title: Insurance industry is moving towards hyper-personalised products, says Niva Bupa deputy CEO Kharbanda- Moneycontrol.com

Generative AI could enable customers to understand policy terms in vernacular languages and use WhatsApp to check coverage or get a simple summary of key policy features, says Kharbanda   September 15, 2026 / 17:30 IST             India’s insurance industry is moving from broad customer segmentation towards more personalised insurance solutions, with technology and generative AI enabling insurers to tailor products, Niva Bupa Health Insurance executive director and deputy CEO Ankur Kharbanda has said. Speaking during a panel discussion on “Building the Insurance Trust Gap” at the GFF Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai on September 10, Kharbanda said while insurance penetration still remains relatively low, the industry has traditionally focused on serving the mass market. "But technology is now making it possible to create more targeted solutions for specific customer profiles," he said. Generative AI could also help customers interact with their policies in a language they understand, he said. Customers could potentially use WhatsApp or similar interfaces to ask whether a particular medical situation is covered, or simply ask for the three most important things they need to know about a policy. Trust starts at point of sale Kharbanda said the trust gap typically emerges when there is a mismatch between what a customer believes they have bought and what the insurer is providing. Insurers need to communicate key information repeatedly at the time of sale, so that customer expectations are aligned with what the policy will deliver, particularly because health insurance may be purchased today but used several years later, he said. Niva Bupa has been investing in training advisers, sales teams and digital callers through an insurance academy, using videos and other visual formats to make insurance easier to understand, he said. The bigger test of trust, however, comes at the time of a claim. He said the industry has a claims settlement ratio of more than 90 percent, while Niva Bupa's is above 95 percent. Of the claims that are not settled, a large proportion relates to waiting periods, with only a smaller portion arising from differences between customer understanding and claim processing. AI to cut claims friction Insurers are increasingly using AI to reduce friction in the claims journey. Kharbanda said cashless discharge remains a major pain point. While the insurance company may take around two hours and the hospital may take another two to three hours, customers tend to perceive the entire process as an insurance delay. Participating in the discussion, Prudential Health India chief operating officer Abhishek Sarath said simplifying insurance would also require addressing the lack of trust between insurers, customers and the provider ecosystem. Insurers often add complexity to products and terms and conditions because they do not have complete trust in customer behaviour or providers, Sarath said. From segments to hyper-personalisation Kharbanda said the industry is increasingly looking beyond broad demographic segments and developing solutions based on specific customer needs. He cited products targeted at younger customers that combine health insurance with features such as maternity and wellness benefits. For customers in smaller cities, insurers can offer tiered hospital networks that exclude some premium hospitals in return for lower premiums. Similarly, customers with employer-provided health covers of Rs 3 lakh-5 lakh may not necessarily need another conventional top-up. Products with deductibles can provide additional protection at substantially lower premiums while potentially becoming the customer's base cover later, he said. Kharbanda said technology could eventually allow insurers to analyse customer information and recommend the most relevant product rather than asking customers to navigate multiple add-ons and riders themselves. Cyber risk adds another trust challenge Mitigata Insurance Brokers chief insurance officer Bhranti Shah said the trust challenge extends to corporate cyber insurance, particularly as AI adoption creates new vulnerabilities. Ransomware attacks, business interruption and invoicing fraud are increasingly important risks for companies, she said. Shah said brokers also need to help companies understand the technical questions involved in buying cyber insurance, including whether they have endpoint detection, data-loss prevention tools, security operations centres and other controls. Incorrect answers can result in a risk being rejected at underwriting or create problems at the time of a claim, she said. The first few hours after a cyber breach are particularly critical. Shah said Mitigata's digital forensics teams have helped around 30-40 clients either avert cyber attacks or negotiate ransomware incidents, adding that the firm has not paid a ransomware demand in these cases. September 15, 2026 / 17:30 IST

India’s insurance industry is moving from broad customer segmentation towards more personalised insurance solutions, with technology and generative AI enabling insurers to tailor products, Niva Bupa Health Insurance executive director and deputy CEO Ankur Kharbanda has said.

Speaking during a panel discussion on “Building the Insurance Trust Gap” at the GFF Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai on September 10, Kharbanda said while insurance penetration still remains relatively low, the industry has traditionally focused on serving the mass market. "But technology is now making it possible to create more targeted solutions for specific customer profiles," he said.

Generative AI could also help customers interact with their policies in a language they understand, he said. Customers could potentially use WhatsApp or similar interfaces to ask whether a particular medical situation is covered, or simply ask for the three most important things they need to know about a policy.

Trust starts at point of sale

Kharbanda said the trust gap typically emerges when there is a mismatch between what a customer believes they have bought and what the insurer is providing.

Insurers need to communicate key information repeatedly at the time of sale, so that customer expectations are aligned with what the policy will deliver, particularly because health insurance may be purchased today but used several years later, he said.

Niva Bupa has been investing in training advisers, sales teams and digital callers through an insurance academy, using videos and other visual formats to make insurance easier to understand, he said.

The bigger test of trust, however, comes at the time of a claim.

He said the industry has a claims settlement ratio of more than 90 percent, while Niva Bupa's is above 95 percent. Of the claims that are not settled, a large proportion relates to waiting periods, with only a smaller portion arising from differences between customer understanding and claim processing.

AI to cut claims friction

Insurers are increasingly using AI to reduce friction in the claims journey.

Kharbanda said cashless discharge remains a major pain point. While the insurance company may take around two hours and the hospital may take another two to three hours, customers tend to perceive the entire process as an insurance delay.

Participating in the discussion, Prudential Health India chief operating officer Abhishek Sarath said simplifying insurance would also require addressing the lack of trust between insurers, customers and the provider ecosystem.

Insurers often add complexity to products and terms and conditions because they do not have complete trust in customer behaviour or providers, Sarath said.

From segments to hyper-personalisation

Kharbanda said the industry is increasingly looking beyond broad demographic segments and developing solutions based on specific customer needs.

He cited products targeted at younger customers that combine health insurance with features such as maternity and wellness benefits. For customers in smaller cities, insurers can offer tiered hospital networks that exclude some premium hospitals in return for lower premiums.

Similarly, customers with employer-provided health covers of Rs 3 lakh-5 lakh may not necessarily need another conventional top-up. Products with deductibles can provide additional protection at substantially lower premiums while potentially becoming the customer's base cover later, he said.

Kharbanda said technology could eventually allow insurers to analyse customer information and recommend the most relevant product rather than asking customers to navigate multiple add-ons and riders themselves.

Cyber risk adds another trust challenge

Mitigata Insurance Brokers chief insurance officer Bhranti Shah said the trust challenge extends to corporate cyber insurance, particularly as AI adoption creates new vulnerabilities.

Ransomware attacks, business interruption and invoicing fraud are increasingly important risks for companies, she said.

Shah said brokers also need to help companies understand the technical questions involved in buying cyber insurance, including whether they have endpoint detection, data-loss prevention tools, security operations centres and other controls.

Incorrect answers can result in a risk being rejected at underwriting or create problems at the time of a claim, she said.

The first few hours after a cyber breach are particularly critical. Shah said Mitigata's digital forensics teams have helped around 30-40 clients either avert cyber attacks or negotiate ransomware incidents, adding that the firm has not paid a ransomware demand in these cases.
